title: The Stonecutter's Milk: Caprese to the Dome of St Peter's
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Caprese, Settignano, and the Stonecutter's Milk

stops.name: Caprese, the podesta's second son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birth date is fixed by the family record kept by Lodovico himself
stops.campa: Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni holds the podesteria of Caprese and Chiusi della Verna, a six-month magistracy over two poor communes in the hills of the upper Tiber above Arezzo. In the Casa del Podesta his second son is born on the sixth of March and christened Michelangelo. The family is old, proud, and short of money; Lodovico counts the Buonarroti Simoni among the respectable houses of Florence and means his sons to keep them there. Within weeks the term ends and the household goes back down to Florence.
suggested_refs: The Casa del Podesta at Caprese Michelangelo, seat of Lodovico's six-month magistracy
sources: Ascanio Condivi, Vita di Michelangelo Buonarroti (1553)

stops.name: La Verna, the mountain inside his father's jurisdiction
stops.date_confidence: unattested as a visit; the date is his birth date, used here only to place the sanctuary inside the six months of Lodovico's writ
stops.campa: The other half of Lodovico's jurisdiction is the commune of Chiusi della Verna, and above it stands the mountain that Count Orlando gave to Francis of Assisi, where in 1224 the stigmata came down. Nothing in Condivi and nothing in Vasari puts the infant, or the man, on that rock, and no convent register of a visit has been found. The ridge stands a few hours' ride from the room where he is born, inside the six months his father governs the commune under it. Whether anyone in that household ever went up is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan sanctuary of La Verna, in the commune of Chiusi della Verna, half of Lodovico Buonarroti's podesteria in 1475
sources: Gap: absent from Condivi (1553) and Vasari (1568 ed.)

stops.name: Settignano, the wet nurse in the quarry village
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the fostering is attested, the month is not
stops.campa: The child is given out to a wet nurse at Settignano, a village of quarrymen on the hills east of Florence. Her husband is a stonecutter who works Buonarroti marble, and the boy stays there through infancy among the tools and the dust. His mother Francesca di Neri dies when he is six, and the family that raised him through infancy is a family of hammers. Long afterwards, talking to Giorgio Vasari, who came from Arezzo as he did, he puts the whole of his vocation down to that kitchen and that milk.
stops.quote: George, if I possess anything of good in my mental constitution, it comes from my having been born in your keen climate of Arezzo; just as I drew the chisel and the mallet with which I carve statues in together with my nurse's milk.
stops.quote_source: Michelangelo to Vasari, reported in Vasari's Life; John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. I
suggested_refs: The Buonarroti quarry holdings at Settignano, worked by the family of his foster father
sources: Symonds, Life of Michelangelo, Ch. I

stops.name: Florence, the grammar school and the beatings
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Condivi and Vasari give no year, only that it precedes the 1488 apprenticeship
stops.campa: Back in the Santa Croce quarter, in the family houses on the Via de' Bentaccordi, he is put to grammar under Francesco da Urbino to be made fit for the wool trade or a notary's desk. He learns little Latin. He goes into the churches instead and copies what is on the walls, and takes beatings for it from his father and his uncles, who hold that a Buonarroti who draws has come down in the world. The beatings do not work. He is thirteen when they give in.
stops.quote: This brought the boy into disfavour with his father and uncles, who often used to beat him severely; for, being insensible to the excellence and nobility of Art, they thought it shameful to give her shelter in their house.
stops.quote_source: Condivi, translated in John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. I
suggested_refs: The Buonarroti houses on the Via de' Bentaccordi, Santa Croce quarter
sources: Symonds, Life of Michelangelo, Ch. I

segments.name: The Print, the Bottega, and the Garden

stops.name: Colmar, the engraving of the tormented hermit
stops.date_confidence: range; the plate is dated c. 1470-1475 and the year here is a placeholder inside that range
stops.campa: In an Alsatian workshop Martin Schongauer cuts a copperplate of Saint Anthony carried up into the air by demons, each one a different composite beast, all of them gripping and beating the hermit while his face stays level. The sheet travels wherever a sheet can travel: to Nuremberg, into the Netherlands, over the Alps into Italian shops where boys are set to copy prints as an exercise. In one of those shops a Florentine apprentice turns the engraving into a painted panel of his own. Schongauer dies in 1491.
suggested_refs: Martin Schongauer, The Temptation of Saint Anthony, engraving, Colmar, c. 1470-1475
sources: Kimbell Art Museum technical and attribution materials

stops.name: Florence, the Torment of Saint Anthony
stops.date_confidence: disputed; dated c. 1487-1488 on style and on Vasari's notice of a Schongauer copy, and the attribution of this particular panel is not universally accepted
stops.campa: Francesco Granacci, a friend from the shop, shows him the Schongauer sheet, and the boy makes it a panel in tempera and oil: the same demons, the same hoisted saint, with a landscape the engraver never gave them and pearl scales on the monsters' hides. Condivi says he went down to the fish market to see how scales take the light. Vasari says only that he copied the German. He is twelve or thirteen. Four panel paintings in all survive from his hand and this is the first.
stops.quote: Granacci happened to show him a print of S. Antonio tormented by the devils. This was the work of Martino d'Olanda, a good artist for the times in which he lived; and Michelangelo transferred the composition to a panel.
stops.quote_source: Condivi and Vasari, translated in John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. I
suggested_refs: The Torment of Saint Anthony, panel, Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth

stops.name: Ghirlandaio's workshop, the contract of the first of April
stops.date_confidence: attested; the contract survives in the Archivio Buonarroti in Lodovico's hand
stops.campa: On the first of April Lodovico writes his son into the shop of Domenico and Davide Ghirlandaio, the largest fresco workshop in Florence, for three years. The terms run the wrong way. Instead of the family paying for training, the boy is to be paid twenty-four florins over the term, and within a year the arrangement is amended again in his favour. He stays about one of the three years. For the rest of his life he tells anyone who asks that he learned nothing there.
stops.quote: I record this first of April how I, Lodovico di Lionardo di Buonarrota, bind my son Michelangelo to Domenico and Davit di Tommaso...
stops.quote_source: Lodovico Buonarroti's own record, 1488, quoted in John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. I
suggested_refs: The Ghirlandaio apprenticeship contract, Archivio Buonarroti, Florence
sources: Archivio Buonarroti contract, cited by Vasari and by Michael Hirst
Symonds, Life of Michelangelo, Ch. I

stops.name: Giardino di San Marco, the faun and the Medici table
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Condivi and Vasari agree on the episode and disagree on its year
stops.campa: Lorenzo de' Medici asks Ghirlandaio for his two best boys and is sent Michelangelo and Granacci. In the garden by San Marco, among antique fragments, Bertoldo di Giovanni, who trained under Donatello, sets them to work in marble. Lorenzo looks at a faun's head the boy has cut, remarks that a man so old would be missing teeth, and comes back to find a tooth knocked out and the gum broken open. He takes him into the Palazzo Medici to eat with Ficino and Poliziano, and with the two boys who will be Leo X and Clement VII.
stops.quote: Oh, you have made this Faun quite old, and yet have left him all his teeth! Do you not know that men of that great age are always wanting in one or two?
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici, reported by Condivi, translated in John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. I
suggested_refs: The Medici sculpture garden by San Marco and the antique collection Bertoldo taught from

stops.name: Santo Spirito, the crucifix and the dissecting room
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Condivi places it after Lorenzo's death in April 1492, without a month
stops.campa: Lorenzo dies in April 1492 and the household that fed him closes. Niccolo Bichiellini, prior of Santo Spirito, gives the seventeen-year-old a room and the bodies out of the convent hospital, and he opens them to find where the muscles begin and end. In return he carves a wooden Christ for the church, painted, life-size, light enough for two men to carry. Pietro Torrigiano, a fellow pupil from the garden, breaks his nose with a fist about this time, and the flattened bridge is in every portrait made of him afterwards.
stops.quote: His prolonged habits of dissection injured his stomach to such an extent that he lost the power of eating or drinking to any profit.
stops.quote_source: Condivi, summarized in John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242)
suggested_refs: The polychrome wooden Crucifix of Santo Spirito, Florence
sources: Benvenuto Cellini's autobiography, for Torrigiano's own boast

segments.name: Flight, Bologna, and the First Rome

stops.name: Venice, the first flight north
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1494 by Condivi; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: With Charles VIII on the road and Savonarola preaching the scourge, Michelangelo leaves Florence some weeks before the Medici are driven out of it. He goes north to Venice with two companions and finds no work there. The account that reaches Condivi is of a young man moving on omens and warnings as much as on news from the road. He turns south again before winter, out of money, and is stopped at Bologna, where a foreigner entering without the wax thumb-seal is fined and he cannot pay the fine.
suggested_refs: The Bolognese entry-seal ordinance that made him a debtor on arrival

stops.name: San Domenico, Bologna: three figures for the Arca
stops.date_confidence: attested by Bolognese payment records to 1494-1495; the month is not fixed
stops.campa: Gianfrancesco Aldrovandi pays the fine and takes him into his house for a year, where in the evenings the young Florentine reads Dante and Petrarch aloud in his own accent. The shrine of Saint Dominic has stood unfinished since Niccolo dell'Arca died. It wants a kneeling angel with a candlestick, a Saint Petronius, a Saint Proculus, and he cuts all three, fitting his hand to a monument Nicola Pisano began two centuries earlier. He studies Jacopo della Quercia's reliefs on the front of San Petronio as well; readers of the Sistine ceiling have found them there fifteen years on. He never says so himself.
suggested_refs: The Arca di San Domenico, Bologna, with Michelangelo's angel, Petronius, and Proculus

stops.name: Florence, the sleeping Cupid sold as an antique
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Condivi and Vasari differ on who did what, and neither gives a month
stops.campa: Back in Florence under the new republic he carves a small marble Cupid asleep. Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici sends it to Rome through a dealer, who buries it, ages it, and sells it to Cardinal Raffaele Riario as an antique; both the sculptor and the man who sent it are cheated of the real price. Riario learns he has bought a modern work, is impressed by it, and sends to Florence for whoever made it. Condivi and Vasari tell the fraud differently and disagree about who aged the marble and who knew.
suggested_refs: The lost sleeping Cupid, sold to Cardinal Riario as an antique in 1496

stops.name: Rome, Riario's commission and the Bacchus
stops.date_confidence: attested; he enters Rome 25 June 1496 and begins the commission on 4 July
stops.campa: He enters Rome for the first time on the twenty-fifth of June, twenty-one years old, and eight days later begins a commission for Riario: a Bacchus in marble, over life-size, unsteady on his feet, the cup held high and the eyes already gone out of focus. Riario refuses it when it is finished. Jacopo Galli, the banker who has stood guarantor for the young Florentine, takes the statue into his own garden and sets it among real antiquities, where visitors take it for one more of them.
suggested_refs: The Bacchus in Jacopo Galli's antique garden near Campo de' Fiori

stops.name: Old St Peter's, the Pieta and the only signature
stops.date_confidence: attested; contracted August 1498, finished 1499 or early 1500, the completion month unrecorded
stops.campa: Jean Bilheres de Lagraulas, cardinal of Saint-Denis and France's ambassador to the papacy, contracts in August 1498 for a marble Virgin with the dead Christ across her knees, at four hundred and fifty gold ducats, for his tomb chapel. Michelangelo is twenty-three signing and twenty-four finishing. Asked why the mother looks younger than the son, he answers that chastity keeps a body fresh. Lombards in the basilica credit the group to Cristoforo Solari, and that night he shuts himself in and cuts his name across the band on her breast.
stops.quote: It is said that certain Lombards passing by and admiring the Pieta ascribed it to Christoforo Solari of Milan, surnamed Il Gobbo. Michelangelo, having happened to overhear them, shut himself up in the chapel, and engraved the belt upon the Madonna's breast with his own name.
stops.quote_source: John Addington Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242), Ch. II, sec. VII; Symonds himself hedges with 'It is said'
suggested_refs: The 1498 Pieta contract for the chapel of Santa Petronilla, Old St Peter's
sources: Pieta contract, August 1498, printed in Symonds, Ch. II

stops.name: Opera del Duomo, the block nobody could use
stops.date_confidence: attested; commission dated 16 August 1501, first cutting 13 September 1501
stops.campa: The Consuls of the Wool Guild and the cathedral works own a block of Carrara marble nine braccia high, quarried forty years earlier, roughed out and abandoned by Agostino di Duccio, left in the yard to weather. Antonio Rossellino is named as a second hand that took it on and gave it up. On the sixteenth of August the commission goes to Michelangelo; on the thirteenth of September he starts cutting. He works behind a boarded enclosure for better than two years and sleeps in the yard in his boots.
suggested_refs: The Opera del Duomo yard behind Florence Cathedral, where the block had stood since the 1460s

stops.name: Piazza della Signoria, David set at the palace door
stops.date_confidence: attested, and two-stage: the figure is installed at the palace entrance in June 1504 and formally unveiled on 8 September 1504
stops.campa: A committee of thirty, with Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli and Filippino Lippi among them, argues in January about where the thing should stand, and the cathedral roofline it was cut for is dropped. Forty men take four days to roll it on greased beams from the works to the piazza. In June it goes up at the door of the Palazzo della Signoria in the place of Donatello's Judith, and it is unveiled in form on the eighth of September: David before the stone is thrown, not after, facing the road that comes from Rome.
suggested_refs: The committee deliberation of 25 January 1504, Archivio di Stato di Firenze
sources: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, 1504 deliberation

stops.name: Palazzo Vecchio, the Battle of Cascina
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1504 by the payment records; the exact date of commission is not fixed
stops.campa: The Signoria sets him to fresco one wall of the Great Council chamber with the Battle of Cascina, Florentine soldiers scrambling naked out of the Arno at the alarm, while Leonardo works the wall opposite with the Battle of Anghiari. Michelangelo finishes the full-size cartoon and nothing beyond it. Painters come to copy it for years and Cellini calls it the school of the world; then it is cut into pieces and scattered. Neither wall is ever painted. Both compositions survive only in other men's copies.
suggested_refs: Aristotile da Sangallo's grisaille copy after the lost Cascina cartoon, Holkham Hall

segments.name: Julius II: the Quarry, the Quarrel, the Vault

stops.name: Carrara, eight months choosing marble for a tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1505 by his own letters; the month is approximate
stops.campa: Julius II, newly elected and building for his own memory, calls him to Rome and orders a freestanding tomb of some forty figures, three storeys, to stand inside St Peter's. Michelangelo goes up into the Apuan Alps and stays the better part of a year, walking the quarry faces, marking blocks for a monument nobody has yet agreed where to put. His letters home are about oxen, barges, and money owed. He will come back to these mountains for thirty years, for tombs and facades that mostly never get built.
suggested_refs: Il Carteggio di Michelangelo, the Carrara letters of 1505

stops.name: Florence, turned away and gone by nightfall
stops.date_confidence: attested; his own account and Condivi's agree on the day
stops.campa: The marble reaches Rome and sits in the piazza of St Peter's at his own expense while the pope, now pouring money into Bramante's rebuilding of the basilica, stops paying for the tomb and stops receiving him. On the seventeenth of April a groom turns him away at the door. He goes back to his lodging, sells what he owns, and rides for Florence the same night. Julius sends three briefs after him, and the Signoria, unwilling to go to war with a pope over one man, hands him back under the cover of an embassy.
stops.quote: You may tell the Pope that, henceforward, if he wants me he must look for me elsewhere.
stops.quote_source: Michelangelo to the papal servant who turned him away, reported by Condivi; Charles Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #19332), Ch. IV
suggested_refs: The three papal briefs sent after him to Florence, spring 1506
sources: Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti, Ch. IV

stops.name: Bologna, the bronze pope and the cannon
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the reconciliation is dated to Julius's occupation of Bologna in late 1506, the casting runs through 1507 into February 1508
stops.campa: Julius takes Bologna by arms and has the sculptor brought to him there to be forgiven. Reproach and pardon arrive in the same breath, and the commission that follows is a bronze of Julius himself, three times life-size, for the facade of San Petronio. Michelangelo pours it twice, having ruined the first cast, and asks whether the left hand should hold a book. A sword, says the pope, I am no scholar. In 1511 the Bentivoglio partisans pull the statue down and melt it into a cannon they name the Giulia.
stops.quote: You ought to have come to us, and you have waited for us to come to you.
stops.quote_source: Pope Julius II to Michelangelo at Bologna, reported by Condivi; Charles Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #19332), Ch. V
suggested_refs: The lost bronze Julius II of San Petronio, destroyed 1511
sources: Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti, Ch. V

stops.name: Sistine Chapel, the contract of the eighth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested; the contract is dated 8 May 1508
stops.campa: He signs for the ceiling of Sixtus IV's chapel at three thousand ducats, the subject twelve apostles on a starry field. Condivi has it that Bramante pushed the job on him so that a sculptor would fail at fresco in public, and the same account has Michelangelo standing in front of Julius to accuse Bramante of throwing down the ancient columns of old St Peter's to speed the demolition. Bramante's scaffold, hung on ropes through holes in the vault, is useless to him; he builds his own off the wall, and then throws out the apostles.
stops.quote: it was an easy thing to pile brick on brick, but to make such a column was most difficult
stops.quote_source: Michelangelo's charge against Bramante before Julius II, narrated indirectly by Condivi; Charles Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #19332), Ch. VI, translating Condivi sec. XXXVIII
suggested_refs: The Sistine ceiling contract of 8 May 1508
sources: Holroyd, Michael Angelo Buonarroti, Ch. VI

stops.name: Sistine Chapel, the vault uncovered
stops.date_confidence: attested; the first half was shown on 15 August 1511, the whole on 31 October 1512, opened to the public the next morning
stops.campa: Four years on his feet with his head back, the neck set so that he reads letters by holding them above his face. Work stops for the better part of a year in 1510 over money already earned. He paints Genesis backwards, from Noah drunk toward God dividing light, the figures growing larger as he goes and the days of plaster per panel growing fewer. Over five hundred square metres, more than three hundred figures. On the vigil of All Saints in 1512 the last screen comes down, and the pope who ordered it is dead within four months.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's sonnet on painting the vault, 'I've grown a goiter in this drudgery'

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the facade that was never built
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1518 for the contract; the cancellation is March 1520
stops.campa: Leo X, Lorenzo's son, who ate at the same table with him as a boy, hands him the front of the Medici parish church and calls it the mirror of all Italy. Michelangelo takes the whole of it, sculpture and architecture and quarrying and carting alike. Two years go into opening a new marble face at Monte Altissimo above Pietrasanta and building a road down to the sea for the blocks, because the pope will not buy from Carrara. In March 1520 the contract is cancelled. San Lorenzo keeps the rough brick front it already had.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's wooden model for the San Lorenzo facade, Casa Buonarroti
The Monte Altissimo quarry road above Pietrasanta

stops.name: New Sacristy, San Lorenzo: the four that cannot rest
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1520 for the commission; work runs to his departure in 1534 and the chapel is left unassembled
stops.campa: Across the church from the facade that will not be built, the Medici set him to a burial chapel for two dead of no great account, Giuliano duke of Nemours and Lorenzo duke of Urbino. He gives them armour they never wore and puts under them four figures on curved lids too steep to lie on: Day with the face unfinished, Night with her owl and her mask, Dawn waking badly, Dusk going under. He works at it through fourteen years and two expulsions of the family it honours, and walks away leaving the pieces on the floor.
suggested_refs: The New Sacristy of San Lorenzo, with Night, Day, Dawn, and Dusk

stops.name: Laurentian Library, the staircase that spills
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1523 for the commission by Clement VII; some accounts give 1524
stops.campa: For the same pope, in the cloister of San Lorenzo, he raises a library over the monks' quarters: a long reading room in grey pietra serena and white plaster, and in front of it a vestibule where the wall order is turned inside out, columns sunk into the masonry, brackets under them holding nothing at all. The stair comes down into that room in three streams like something poured. He leaves Florence before it is built, sends the design and a clay model to Vasari in the 1550s, Ammannati executes the stairs in 1559, and the library opens in 1571.
suggested_refs: The vestibule and stair of the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, executed by Ammannati 1559
sources: Michelangelo's correspondence with Vasari on the staircase

stops.name: San Miniato al Monte, the tower hung with wool
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1528-1529 by the republic's own records; the month of his appointment as governor general of fortifications is April 1529
stops.campa: The Medici are thrown out again in 1527, and by 1529 the restored republic is besieged by the emperor's army and the pope's together. Michelangelo is made governor general of the fortifications. He throws up earth and brushwood bastions faster than stone can be cut, and hangs the campanile of San Miniato with mattresses of wool to take the artillery, because that tower is the highest gun platform on the south side and the besiegers are working to bring it down. The tower stands. The city does not.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's fortification drawings for the Florentine republic, Casa Buonarroti

stops.name: Venice, the flight to the Giudecca
stops.date_confidence: attested to late September 1529 by Florentine government correspondence; the precise day of arrival is not fixed
stops.campa: In September, having warned the Signoria that the walls are being betrayed from inside and not been believed, he abandons his post and rides north with two companions and several thousand florins sewn into their clothes. In Venice he takes lodgings on the Giudecca and thinks about going on to France, where Francis I has offered him a place. Florence declares him a rebel, then, needing him, offers a pardon. He is back at the bastions by November. The city holds out until the following August.
suggested_refs: The Florentine decree of rebellion against Michelangelo, autumn 1529, and its withdrawal

stops.name: Medici Chapel, the room under the floor
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the hiding is reconstruction from later scholarship around the room found in 1975, not from a contemporary document
stops.campa: Florence falls, the Medici come back, and Clement VII has reason to remember who built the walls against him. Tradition holds that Michelangelo hid about two months in a chamber under the New Sacristy, seven metres by two, reached through a trapdoor, and covered its plaster in charcoal and chalk: a torso, a pair of legs, a horse, a head that repeats the Giuliano he had carved in the room above. The pope pardoned him and put him back on the tombs. The chamber was found in 1975 and opened to visitors in 2023.
suggested_refs: The charcoal drawings in the chamber beneath the New Sacristy, rediscovered 1975
sources: Later scholarship on the 1975 discovery; no contemporary document attests the hiding

stops.name: Rome, Tommaso de' Cavalieri
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1532 by the surviving correspondence; the month of the meeting is not recorded
stops.campa: In Rome he meets Tommaso de' Cavalieri, a Roman nobleman of about twenty-three. He is fifty-seven. He sends him presentation drawings made to be kept and not sold, Ganymede carried up by the eagle, Tityus with the bird at his liver, and the largest run of poems he ever addressed to one person; some three hundred sonnets and madrigals survive from his hand altogether. Cavalieri answers in the formal register of a young nobleman thanking a great one, and goes on answering for thirty-two years.
suggested_refs: The presentation drawings for Cavalieri: the Rape of Ganymede and the Punishment of Tityus
sources: Michelangelo's Rime and his letters to Cavalieri (Carteggio)

stops.name: Macel de' Corvi, the house under the Capitoline
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1534; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He leaves Florence in September with the Medici tombs unfinished and does not go back for the thirty years he has left. In Rome he takes a house on the Macel de' Corvi under the Capitoline, near Trajan's column, with a garden, some hens, and a servant. Clement VII dies two days after he arrives, which cancels the work he came for. Paul III is elected within weeks, comes to the house in person with cardinals in train, and tells him he has wanted this for thirty years and will not be refused now.
suggested_refs: The house on Macel de' Corvi, demolished for the Vittorio Emanuele II monument

stops.name: Piazza del Campidoglio, the hill turned around
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1536 for the start of the design; construction runs for a century after
stops.campa: Paul III sets him to the hill where the Roman republic once kept its records, then a muddy slope with the senators' palace facing the wrong way, out over the ruins of the forum. Michelangelo turns the whole composition round to face St Peter's, puts the ancient bronze Marcus Aurelius at the centre on a base of his own design, angles two palace fronts to open a trapezoid instead of a square, and draws an oval pavement of twelve points. The pavement is laid in 1940. The facades go up to his drawings over the hundred years after his death.
suggested_refs: The Capitoline oval pavement, drawn by Michelangelo and laid in 1940

stops.name: San Silvestro in Capite, Vittoria Colonna
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the friendship is generally dated from about 1536 to her death in 1547, without a first meeting on record
stops.campa: Vittoria Colonna, marchioness of Pescara, widowed young, lodges at the convent of San Silvestro and writes verse on the reform of the Church in company with men who will shortly be investigated for it. Michelangelo makes her drawings of the Crucifixion and a Pieta meant for her alone and not for sale, and they trade sonnets on grace and the blood of Christ for eleven years. She outranks him by a long way socially and answers his sonnets with her own. When she dies in 1547 he says the thing he cannot get over is that he kissed her hand and not her face.
suggested_refs: The Crucifixion and Pieta drawings made for Vittoria Colonna
sources: Michelangelo's Rime, the sonnets to Vittoria Colonna

stops.name: Sistine Chapel, the Last Judgment on the altar wall
stops.date_confidence: attested; commissioned by Clement VII in 1533-34, confirmed by Paul III, painted 1536-1541 and unveiled 31 October 1541
stops.campa: Clement VII orders the altar wall painted and dies; Paul III holds him to it. Two of his own lunettes and an altarpiece by Perugino come down, the wall is rebuilt to lean outward so it will shed dust, and he paints for five years a Christ who stands up to judge with his arm raised and no throne under him. Saint Bartholomew holds a flayed skin with the painter's own face on it. Biagio da Cesena calls the whole thing fit for a bathhouse and finds himself down in hell with the ears of an ass.
suggested_refs: The flayed skin of Saint Bartholomew, carrying Michelangelo's self-portrait

stops.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, the tragedy of the tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1545 for the completed monument; the six contracts run 1505, 1513, 1516, 1532, 1542, 1545
stops.campa: The tomb of Julius II is contracted six times across forty years and shrinks at every signing, from a freestanding mausoleum of forty figures in the middle of St Peter's to a wall monument in the dead pope's old titular church. What goes up in 1545 carries his Moses, horned from the Vulgate's reading of the shining face in Exodus, with Rachel and Leah at either side and work by other hands above. The bound slaves cut for the first design never reach this wall; two of them stand in Paris. He called the business the tragedy of the tomb.
suggested_refs: The Moses of San Pietro in Vincoli
The Dying Slave and Rebellious Slave, Louvre, cut for the abandoned first design

stops.name: St Peter's, the drum built so the dome cannot be argued away
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1546, following Sangallo's death on 3 August 1546; the appointment is confirmed by papal brief in January 1547
stops.campa: Antonio da Sangallo the Younger dies and the pope makes Michelangelo architect of St Peter's. He is seventy-one and takes no salary, saying that the work is for God and for the good of his own soul. He throws out Sangallo's model, goes back toward Bramante's Greek cross, thickens the piers until they will carry what he means to put on them, and designs a dome on a high drum with paired columns and ribs. He gets the drum up before he dies. Della Porta later raises the vault steeper than the model, and it is closed in 1590.
suggested_refs: Michelangelo's wooden model for the dome of St Peter's, Fabbrica di San Pietro
sources: Construction records of the Fabbrica di San Pietro

stops.name: Palazzo Farnese, the cornice
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1546; the month of the appointment is not fixed
stops.campa: The Farnese palace is Sangallo's too, and also inherited, and the argument is the cornice. Sangallo's design had been faulted as too slight for the mass under it. Michelangelo builds one heavier than anyone expects, thrown far out over the street, a Farnese lily at its centre. He redesigns the top storey and cuts the middle window into a balcony over the piazza. In 1911 a bronze man with no head and no arms, made by Auguste Rodin, is stood in the courtyard beneath that cornice.
suggested_refs: The Farnese cornice, and Rodin's Walking Man installed beneath it in 1911

stops.name: Macel de' Corvi, the last fever
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death is reported the same week in Daniele da Volterra's letter to Vasari
stops.campa: He is working on the Rondanini Pieta within days of the end, a Christ and a mother cut back twice out of an earlier version until the two of them are nearly one body. On the eighteenth of February he dies in the house under the Capitoline of a slow fever, three weeks short of eighty-nine. In the room are Tommaso de' Cavalieri, Daniele da Volterra, Diomede Leoni, two physicians, and his servant Antonio del Franzese. He leaves his soul to God, his body to the earth, and his goods to his nearest kin.
suggested_refs: Daniele da Volterra's letter to Vasari reporting the death and naming those present

stops.name: Santa Croce, the body brought home in a bale
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1564 for the arrival in Florence; sources differ by a day or two on the date
stops.campa: Pius IV means to bury him in St Peter's. His nephew Leonardo Buonarroti and the city of Florence want him back, and the body leaves Rome in a bale entered as merchandise, reaching Florence in the second week of March. The Accademia del Disegno, founded that same year, gives him a funeral in San Lorenzo with an oration and painted panels made for the occasion. Vasari designs the tomb in Santa Croce, Painting and Sculpture and Architecture sitting under the bust. It is finished in the 1570s.
suggested_refs: Vasari's tomb for Michelangelo in Santa Croce, with figures by Lorenzi, Cioli, and Bandini
sources: Vasari, Le Vite (1568 ed.), who organized the funeral

stops.name: Casa Buonarroti, the pronouns changed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1623 for the first printed edition; no month needed
stops.campa: His grand-nephew, Michelangelo Buonarroti the Younger, prints the poems for the first time fifty-nine years after the death. He smooths the metre, drops what he finds obscure, and changes the gender of the pronouns in the poems written to Tommaso de' Cavalieri so that they read as addressed to a woman. That edition stands for two centuries. John Addington Symonds goes back to the manuscripts in the 1870s and prints what was actually written, in the same years he is arguing in private pamphlets for the men those poems were for.
suggested_refs: The 1623 Rime edited by Michelangelo Buonarroti the Younger; Symonds's later restoration from manuscript
sources: Symonds, The Life of Michelangelo Buonarroti (Gutenberg #11242)

stops.name: Galleria dell'Accademia, David walked through the streets
stops.date_confidence: attested; the move runs 30 July to 10 August 1873
stops.campa: Three and a half centuries in the open have opened cracks in the left leg, and the ankles are carrying weight the sculptor never meant them to carry alone. Between the thirtieth of July and the tenth of August the figure is walked across Florence in a wheeled wooden crate running on rails, eleven days for under a kilometre. It waits in a shed at the Accademia until the rotunda built for it is ready in 1882. A marble copy takes the place at the palace door in 1910.
suggested_refs: The 1873 transport crate and rails, and the Accademia tribune built for David in 1882

stops.name: New Sacristy, Rodin in front of the Medici tombs
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 April 1875 by Rodin's own correspondence
stops.campa: Auguste Rodin, thirty-four and paying for the trip himself, comes down into Italy and on the fifteenth of April stands in the New Sacristy, in a chapel its sculptor left unassembled. He draws the four figures from memory at night in his room. He goes back north to make a man standing wrong on purpose, and to leave his own marble rough where the chisel stopped, the way these four are left. What he writes home from Florence is that Michelangelo has freed him from the academy.
suggested_refs: Rodin's 1875 letters from Florence on the Medici tombs

stops.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, Freud in front of the Moses
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is fixed by Freud's own letters
stops.campa: Sigmund Freud, forty-five, reaches Rome after years of finding reasons not to go, and on the tenth of September stands in San Pietro in Vincoli in front of the Moses. He returns on every Roman trip after that. In September 1913 he spends three weeks measuring and sketching the figure daily, and in 1914 publishes an essay anonymously arguing that the man is not about to rise in fury but has just that instant decided not to, holding the tablets and his own rage in the same grip.
suggested_refs: Freud, 'The Moses of Michelangelo' (1914), published anonymously in Imago

stops.name: St Peter's, fifteen blows of a hammer
stops.date_confidence: attested; Pentecost Sunday, 21 May 1972
stops.campa: On Pentecost Sunday a Hungarian-born Australian geologist named Laszlo Toth climbs the rail with a hammer under his coat, shouting that he is Christ risen from the dead, and lands fifteen blows before bystanders drag him off. The Virgin loses her left arm at the elbow, part of the nose, an eyelid, a piece of the veil. Fragments leave the basilica in tourists' pockets and some of them come back. The restored group has stood behind glass ever since, the barrier renewed again in 2024 for the Jubilee.
suggested_refs: The 1972 restoration of the Pieta and its bulletproof screen

stops.name: Sistine Chapel, fourteen years of cleaning
stops.date_confidence: attested to a 1980-1994 campaign; the start month is not needed here
stops.campa: Restorers start on the lunettes and work fourteen years across the vault, lifting off candle soot, animal glue brushed on as varnish by earlier hands, and the smoke of every conclave held beneath it. What comes out underneath is a palette nobody alive had seen: acid green, orange, shot pink. Some scholars argue loudly that the cleaners have taken away the painter's own last shadows worked in secco. The same campaign exposes the giornate, the day-sized patches of fresh plaster, so his pace can be counted panel by panel.
suggested_refs: The 1980-1994 Vatican restoration and the giornate map of the ceiling

stops.name: Fort Worth, the panel gets its name back
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2009 for the Kimbell acquisition and announcement; the 2008 sale is dated July
stops.campa: A panel of Saint Anthony hoisted into the air by demons sells at Sotheby's in London in 2008 as workshop of Ghirlandaio, for about two million dollars. The buyer sends it to the Metropolitan Museum, where cleaning and infrared turn up underdrawing and changes of mind that no copyist would make. The Kimbell Art Museum buys it in 2009 and hangs it as Michelangelo's earliest surviving painting, made at twelve or thirteen after a German engraving. No document ties the panel to him. The attribution rests on what Condivi and Vasari say and on what the infrared shows, and not every specialist accepts it.
suggested_refs: The Torment of Saint Anthony, Kimbell Art Museum, acquired 2009
sources: Kimbell Art Museum acquisition and technical record
